catalog_locator: Ch.2 §2.2 'Prosodic Units' p.43; §2.2.1.1 pp.43-44; §2.2.1.4 'Identification of Contrastive Tones' pp.45-46; ch.5 §5.2 'Sentence Phonology' p.108; §5.2.2.2-5.2.2.3 pp.115-116.
catalog_quote: The vocalic sounds discussed thus far do not occur alone within the syllable structure. They appear with prosodic units called tones. In fact, like the vast majority of African languages, Koshin shows a prosodic contrast of tones. Beside tones, other prosodic units are attested: the prosodies of labialization and coronalization (palatalization). Nasalization prosody is also attested. However, unlike the other prosodic features which occur lexically, nasalization is attested only on the phrasal level. ... Koshin language shows three level tones, which are usually carried by vowels but sometimes by nasal consonants. Some falling and rising tones are attested. But they are regarded as mere association of level tones. ... It should be observed from examples (16) that tones have a lexical value in Koshin. In other words, the two members of the minimal pairs of tone identified thus far contrast in terms of their meaning, not in terms of their grammatical characteristics. However, tones can also have a grammatical value in the language as attested in (17) below ... [p.108] The syllable and the prosodic word domains (on a par with the “foot” in languages where it is relevant) are considered minor prosodic constituents within the well established prosodic hierarchy.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (extracted text of the PDF we hold; page numbers cross-checked against the PDF with extracted text/-l). (1) Quote: all three fragments are present verbatim. 'The vocalic sounds discussed thus far do not occur alone within the syllable structure. They appear with prosodic units called tones. In fact, like the vast majority of African languages, Koshin shows a prosodic contrast of tones. Nasalization prosody is also attested.' opens section 2.2 'Prosodic Units' on p.43 (p.61; the text); 'Koshin language shows three level tones, which are usually carried by vowels…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Koshin is described as a tone language with three contrastive level tones (H, M, L; contours = sequences of levels), tone having both lexical and grammatical (e.g. cl.9/10 sg/pl) function. The 444-page grammar enumerates the language's prosodic units as tone, labialization, palatalization and (phrasal) nasalization and never mentions word stress or accent; the only nod is that the metrical foot is a constituent 'in languages where it is relevant', implicitly not Koshin. No statement of stress position exists in the primary description.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The grammar does document stem-initial positional privilege (labialization/coronalization affect only the onset of the first syllable of the prosodic word, pp.74-75; in disyllabic verb roots the second syllable admits only the vowels a/ə and is the only place L tone occurs, p.152), the same kind of evidence Lovegren 2012 analyses as abstract stem-initial accent in neighbouring Mungbam, but Ousmanou does not draw that conclusion.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level prosody = tone; the only 'prominence' discussed is phonological-phrase-level (NP head at left edge of the phonological phrase, pp.115-116), not word stress. Data are citation forms and elicited phrases from Koshin village.
new_statements.identity_note: Ousmanou 2014 describes the speech of Koshin village (Fungom subdivision, Menchum, NW Region), i.e. kosh1246 proper (Glottolog groups it with Bukwen as Koshin-Bukwen kosh1247). Lovegren 2012 is about Mungbam (abar1238/mung1266 area), cited only as areal context.

new_statements.quote: Koshin makes use of at least three contrastive tone levels, in addition to contour tones, with a three-way tonal minimal pair being jùà ‘stream’, jūā ‘bee’, and júá ‘soup’. For the most part, three levels have been sufficient to characterize the encountered tonal distinctions, but there has been some data which suggests that perhaps four levels are warranted. [...] As with the other languages of the area, tonal contours are found, with an example of a fall being found in the word ncê ‘sneeze (n.)’ and a rise in fı᷄ ‘float’. [p.113, Section 3.1, on the Lower Fungom languages generally:] For example, they are all tonal, show basic SVO word order

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement from Ousmanou 2014 (tone language, no stress statement): Koshin is tonal, with a three- (possibly four-) level system plus contours, and no word-stress placement is stated. The catalog record for Koshin has an empty rule, and this work gives nothing that would fill it. the quote was verified verbatim against goodetal2011_persee_pages/ and against the authors' March 2011 pdfTeX preprint (same wording; preprint likewise has no stress/accent statement).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. Koshin is described as a tone language with at least three (possibly four) contrastive tone levels plus falling and rising contours; the article says nothing about word stress, accent or prominence for Koshin (the only occurrences of 'stressed', 'prominence', 'prominent' in the whole article are non-technical: 'it should be stressed that', a village that 'gained prominence', 'one prominent grammatical connection').
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. On tone: possible fourth tone level (Class 9 vs Class 10 subject-pronoun pair in (13), pp.142-143, alternatively analysable as downstep); contours not yet shown to contrast among themselves; verbal tonal inflection 'remains underexplored'.
new_statements.identity_note: Good et al. 2011 describe Koshin as a one-village language of eastern Lower Fungom (village of Koshin), based on Good's fieldwork in 2005, 2007 and 2008 (p.140); the same variety Ousmanou 2014 describes. The article notes that Koshin and Fang were earlier conflated as one language (p.147) but treats them separately; the Koshin data here are not Fang data.
